title: Histopathology Techniques
description: Specimen reception and fixation, tissue processing, microtomy, routine and special staining, frozen sections, immunohistochemistry and laboratory safety.

topics.title: Fixation
topics.summary: Aims of fixation, types of fixatives, factors affecting fixation and common artefacts.

notes.b: Fixation preserves tissue in a life-like state by preventing autolysis (self-digestion by enzymes) and putrefaction (bacterial decay), hardening tissue and preparing it for staining. 10% neutral buffered formalin (4% formaldehyde) is the routine fixative; it cross-links proteins (additive, non-coagulant) and penetrates about 1 mm per hour. The volume of fixative should be 10–20 times the tissue volume. Other fixatives: Bouin's solution (picric acid, formalin, acetic acid — good for testicular and GI biopsies, but lyses red cells), Zenker's and Helly's (mercuric chloride — toxic; for haemopoietic tissue), Carnoy's (alcohol-based, rapid, preserves glycogen and nucleic acids), glutaraldehyde (for electron microscopy), and alcohol (coagulant; used for cytology smears).

Fixation is affected by time (large specimens need 24–48 hours; slice them), temperature, pH (buffered formalin prevents acid formalin pigment), penetration and fixative volume. Unbuffered formalin produces formalin (acid haematin) pigment — dark brown granules — removed with alcoholic picric acid. Mercuric fixatives leave mercury pigment (removed with iodine then sodium thiosulphate). Delayed fixation causes autolysis (poor nuclear staining). Decalcification of bone (with acids such as nitric or formic acid, or chelating agents such as EDTA — slower but gentler, preserving antigens and DNA) follows fixation; the end-point is tested chemically or radiologically.

topics.title: Tissue Processing and Embedding
topics.summary: Dehydration, clearing, infiltration and embedding in paraffin wax.

notes.b: After fixation, tissue is processed so it can be infiltrated with paraffin wax, which is immiscible with water. Dehydration removes water using graded (ascending) alcohols — 70%, 90%, 100% ethanol (or isopropanol). Clearing removes alcohol with a solvent miscible with both alcohol and wax, such as xylene (the commonest; makes tissue transparent), chloroform or toluene. Infiltration (impregnation) replaces the clearing agent with molten paraffin wax (melting point about 56–58 °C) in the oven, often under vacuum. Automated tissue processors perform these steps overnight.
k: Order: fixation → dehydration → clearing → infiltration → embedding

notes.b: Embedding places infiltrated tissue in moulds of molten wax, correctly oriented (e.g. skin and tubular structures on edge to show all layers), to form blocks that are cooled and trimmed. Processing errors: incomplete dehydration leaves water, preventing clearing and wax infiltration (soft, mushy blocks); prolonged dehydration or clearing makes tissue brittle and hard; overheated wax causes shrinkage. Other embedding media: resin for thin sections of hard tissues (bone marrow trephines), celloidin, and gelatin; frozen sections avoid processing entirely.
k: Incomplete dehydration → soft, poorly infiltrated blocks

topics.title: Microtomy and Frozen Sections
topics.summary: Types of microtome, knives, section cutting faults and rapid frozen sections.

notes.b: Microtomes cut thin sections from wax blocks: the rotary microtome (most common for paraffin sections, 3–5 µm), sledge/sliding microtome (large blocks, celloidin), rocking microtome, and ultramicrotome (for electron microscopy, 50–100 nm, with glass or diamond knives). The cryostat is a microtome inside a refrigerated cabinet for frozen sections. Disposable steel blades are now standard. Sections are floated on a warm water bath (about 5–10 °C below the wax melting point) to remove wrinkles, picked up onto clean glass slides (adhesives or charged slides for immunohistochemistry) and dried.
k: Rotary microtome: routine paraffin sections (3–5 µm)
Water bath below wax melting point

notes.b: Sectioning faults: thick and thin sections alternately (loose block or knife, or excessive clearance angle), chattering or vibration (hard tissue, blunt knife), holes in sections (poor processing, calcium), scoring/lines (nicks in the knife edge, calcium or hard particles), and compression. Frozen sections are cut on a cryostat at about −20 °C without processing, allowing rapid intraoperative diagnosis within 10–20 minutes (e.g. deciding whether margins are clear or a lump is malignant) and demonstrating lipids and enzymes (which are lost or inactivated in paraffin processing). Morphology is poorer than in paraffin sections, and ice crystal artefact can occur.
k: Chattering: hard tissue or blunt knife

topics.title: Routine and Special Stains
topics.summary: H&E staining, and special stains for carbohydrates, connective tissue, microorganisms and pigments.

notes.b: Sections are dewaxed in xylene and rehydrated through descending alcohols to water before staining. Haematoxylin (from Haematoxylum campechianum logwood) is oxidised to haematein and used with a mordant (aluminium in Harris's and Mayer's haematoxylin; iron in Weigert's) to stain nuclei blue-black. Progressive staining stains to the desired intensity; regressive staining overstains then differentiates in acid alcohol, followed by 'bluing' in alkaline water (Scott's tap water substitute). Eosin counterstains cytoplasm, collagen and muscle pink/red. Sections are then dehydrated, cleared and mounted (DPX) under a coverslip.
k: Dewax → rehydrate → stain → dehydrate → clear → mount
Regressive: overstain, differentiate in acid alcohol, blue

notes.b: Carbohydrates: periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stains glycogen (removed by diastase digestion), mucins and basement membranes magenta; Alcian blue stains acid mucins. Connective tissue: Van Gieson (collagen red, muscle yellow), Masson's trichrome (collagen blue/green), Verhoeff's (elastic fibres black), reticulin silver stains. Amyloid: Congo red (apple-green birefringence under polarised light). Microorganisms: Ziehl–Neelsen (mycobacteria), Grocott's methenamine silver and PAS (fungi), Giemsa (Helicobacter, parasites), Gram (bacteria). Pigments and minerals: Perls' Prussian blue (haemosiderin iron), Masson–Fontana (melanin), von Kossa (calcium black), rhodanine (copper). Lipids: oil red O and Sudan black on frozen sections.

topics.title: Cytology, Immunohistochemistry and Laboratory Safety
topics.summary: Exfoliative cytology and Pap smears, immunohistochemistry, and hazards in the histology laboratory.

notes.b: Exfoliative cytology examines cells shed from surfaces (cervical Pap smears, sputum, urine, body fluids); fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) samples lumps (thyroid, breast, lymph nodes). Smears for Papanicolaou staining must be fixed immediately in 95% ethanol (wet fixation) to avoid air-drying artefact; air-dried smears are used for Romanowsky (Giemsa/May–Grünwald) stains. Liquid-based cytology improves quality. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses labelled antibodies to detect specific antigens in tissue (e.g. cytokeratin — carcinomas; CD45 — lymphomas; oestrogen receptor and HER2 — breast cancer treatment decisions; Ki-67 — proliferation). Heat-induced epitope retrieval unmasks formalin-cross-linked antigens; the reaction is visualised with chromogens such as DAB (brown). Positive and negative controls are essential.

Hazards in histopathology include formaldehyde (irritant, sensitiser, carcinogen — use fume hoods and monitor exposure), xylene (neurotoxic, flammable), picric acid (explosive when dry — keep moist), mercuric salts (toxic), microtome blades (sharps injuries — use blade guards), infectious specimens (TB, hepatitis, prions — Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease tissue needs special handling), and heat from wax dispensers. Specimens, blocks and slides must be accurately labelled and tracked; blocks and slides are archived for medico-legal and review purposes. Clinical information on request forms helps interpretation.
k: Picric acid: keep moist (explosive when dry)
